nodes.title: IP routing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Routing is how packets find their way through a multi-network internet. Every router runs a forwarding table; routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) are the mechanisms by which routers exchange information and build that table.

flashcards.front: What's the longest-prefix-match rule?
flashcards.back: When multiple routes match a destination, the router picks the one with the most-specific (longest) prefix. So `10.0.0.0/24` beats `10.0.0.0/16` for a packet to `10.0.0.5`. This is how more-specific routes can override defaults.

flashcards.front: Default route — what does `0.0.0.0/0` mean?
flashcards.back: It matches every destination, so it's used only when no more-specific route exists. Typically points to the internet gateway. On a stub network, the default route is often the ONLY route — everything not local goes 'up' to a smarter router.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic routing — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Static routes are hand-configured, easy to understand, perfect for small or stub networks. Dynamic routing (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP) auto-discovers topology, reacts to link failures, scales to thousands of routers. Use dynamic the moment the topology is non-trivial or expected to change.

flashcards.front: Administrative distance — what is it?
flashcards.back: When the same destination is learned from multiple sources (static + OSPF + BGP), the router prefers the one with the lowest administrative distance. Defaults (Cisco): connected=0, static=1, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, BGP=200. It's the tie-breaker before the routing-protocol metric.

questions.q: A router has these routes: 10.0.0.0/8, 10.1.0.0/16, and 10.1.1.0/24. A packet arrives for 10.1.1.5. Which route is selected?
choices: The packet is dropped — multiple matches cause ambiguity
questions.explanation: Routers use longest prefix match. /24 is the most specific (longest) match for 10.1.1.5, so it wins over /16 and /8.

questions.q: Two routes for the same destination are received: one from EIGRP and one from OSPF. The router chooses the EIGRP route because EIGRP's administrative distance (90) is lower than OSPF's. What is OSPF's default AD?
choices: 90 — that's EIGRP internal, not OSPF
110 — OSPF's default AD on Cisco IOS
questions.explanation: OSPF has an AD of 110. EIGRP internal is 90, RIP is 120, and EBGP is 20. Lower AD = more trusted.

questions.q: Six OSPF routers share a broadcast Ethernet segment. The protocol elects two of them — the DR and the BDR — and every other router (DROTHER) flows its LSAs to the DR/BDR via the AllDRouters multicast rather than directly to every neighbour. Why was the DR role introduced?
choices: To reduce flooding overhead on multi-access segments
To assign OSPF router-IDs to neighbours on the segment
To encrypt OSPF Hello packets exchanged between routers
To redistribute OSPF routes into other routing protocols
questions.explanation: Without a DR, every router on the segment would have to form a full adjacency with every other router — an N² problem. The DR (and BDR for redundancy) collects updates and floods them on behalf of the segment, reducing adjacencies to roughly N. Router-ID assignment is automatic, encryption is configured separately, and redistribution is an ASBR responsibility.

questions.q: EIGRP's composite metric formula includes terms for K1..K5 weights. By default Cisco IOS sets K1 = K3 = 1 and K2 = K4 = K5 = 0, which means the default metric is computed from only TWO of the five candidate inputs. Which two?
choices: Bandwidth (K1) and delay (K3) — all other K-values default to 0
Load and reliability — K2 and K5, both 0 by default
Cost and bandwidth — 'cost' is OSPF, not EIGRP
Hop count and MTU — RIP uses hop count, MTU isn't a default EIGRP input
questions.explanation: EIGRP uses bandwidth and delay by default (K1=1, K3=1, others=0). Load and reliability are available but disabled by default as they cause route flapping.

questions.q: Two routers on the same Ethernet broadcast segment must agree on OSPF timers or no adjacency forms. By default on this network type, what is the OSPF Hello interval?
choices: 10 seconds — the default Hello on a broadcast or point-to-point OSPF network
40 seconds — the default DEAD interval (4× Hello), not the Hello
5 seconds
30 seconds — the default Hello on NBMA/point-to-multipoint OSPF networks, not broadcast
questions.explanation: OSPF sends Hello packets every 10 seconds on broadcast/point-to-point links. On NBMA links the default is 30 seconds. The Dead interval is 4× the Hello interval.

questions.q: An engineer is on a router and wants to confirm OSPF adjacency state (INIT / 2WAY / EXSTART / EXCHANGE / LOADING / FULL) with each neighbour, plus their router-id, interface, and DR/BDR role. Which `show` command surfaces exactly that table?
choices: `debug ip ospf hello` — generates a real-time hello-packet trace per interface; it does not display a formatted neighbour-state table showing adjacency, RID, and DR/BDR
`show ip route ospf` — lists OSPF-learned routes, not neighbour state
`show ip ospf database` — dumps LSAs, not the neighbour state table
`show ip ospf neighbor` — prints the OSPF neighbour table (state, RID, interface, DR/BDR)
questions.explanation: 'show ip ospf neighbor' lists all OSPF neighbors, their state (FULL, 2WAY, etc.), router IDs, and interfaces. FULL state means a complete adjacency has formed.

questions.q: A WAN edge router has an OSPF-learned default route (AD 110) via Gi0/0 to the primary ISP. The same router has `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1 254` configured pointing to a backup DSL link. Day-to-day, the OSPF default is installed and the static is not. Then the primary ISP link drops and OSPF withdraws the default. What happens next?
choices: The static AD-254 route was already installed and ignored OSPF; nothing changes on failure
The static AD-254 route would only install if a second OSPF neighbour appears
The static AD-254 route would only install when load-balancing is required
AD-254 static route installs — OSPF default (AD 110) is down, this is the floating-static role
questions.explanation: A floating static route's AD is deliberately set higher than the primary protocol. It only enters the routing table when the primary route (with lower AD) is gone, acting as a backup.

questions.q: Two routers (R1 and R2) sit at the edge of a campus subnet. Hosts on the subnet are configured with a single default gateway 10.0.0.1. R1 and R2 jointly own the virtual IP 10.0.0.1: R1 is currently active, R2 is standby and listens for hello messages. If R1 fails, R2 takes over the virtual MAC and the hosts never notice. Which Cisco protocol is this?
choices: IPsec site-to-site tunnel — an encrypted WAN overlay between two sites; it is not a virtual default-gateway IP shared between two redundant first-hop routers on the same subnet
HSRP — Hot Standby Router Protocol, active/standby virtual-IP gateway redundancy
Dynamic routing protocol — OSPF/EIGRP route between routers, not host default-gateway redundancy
ECMP load-balancing — equal-cost load-sharing, not active/standby gateway failover
questions.explanation: HSRP creates a virtual IP and MAC shared by multiple routers. One is active, others are standby. If the active router fails, a standby takes over — hosts never change their default gateway.

nodes.title: Let VLAN 10 talk to VLAN 20

choices: Router (Layer 3 device)
A second Layer 2 switch
Network hub
Wireless access point

nodes.explanation: VLANs are separate Layer 2 broadcast domains; traffic between them must be routed by a Layer 3 device (a router, router-on-a-stick, or a Layer 3 switch). A Layer 2 switch alone can't move traffic between VLANs.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

pairs.left: A router has 'hostname R1', 'ip domain-name corp.local', a 2048-bit RSA key pair
An admin enables SSH on a Cisco router. Hostname and ip domain-name are already
An attacker connects a tool to a switch port and floods the switch with frames c

correct.useCase: A link-state interior gateway protocol that builds a topology map and runs SPF (Dijkstra) to pick lowest-cost routes; areas keep it scalable.

distractors.useCase: Speeds up frame forwarding inside a single switch.
A standard for forwarding packets between operating systems.
Calculates subnet masks from a host-count requirement.

nodes.title: VLANs: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A VLAN logically segments a single physical switch into multiple broadcast domains. VLAN 10 traffic can't see VLAN 20 traffic without a Layer-3 routed hop, even on the same switch. This is the foundation of multi-tenant networking on shared hardware.

flashcards.front: Access port vs trunk port — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: An access port belongs to exactly one VLAN and strips the tag — end hosts don't see VLAN headers. A trunk port carries multiple VLANs between switches using 802.1Q tags. Hosts plug into access ports; switches connect to each other via trunks.

flashcards.front: What is the native VLAN on a trunk?
flashcards.back: The native VLAN is the one VLAN that's NOT tagged on a trunk — frames in that VLAN traverse the link with no 802.1Q header. Defaults to VLAN 1 but should be changed to an unused VLAN on every trunk for security (prevents VLAN hopping attacks).

flashcards.front: Why use a Layer-3 SVI?
flashcards.back: A Switched Virtual Interface (SVI) gives a VLAN a Layer-3 address inside the switch — it's the inter-VLAN router. Without an SVI (or external router), VLANs can't talk to each other. Modern switches do inter-VLAN routing in hardware at wire speed.

flashcards.front: What's VLAN hopping?
flashcards.back: An attacker tricks the switch into forwarding their traffic into a VLAN they shouldn't be in. Two flavors: double-tagging (exploits the native-VLAN-untagged rule) and switch-spoofing (the host negotiates a trunk via DTP). Mitigation: tag the native VLAN, set ports to access mode explicitly, disable DTP.

questions.q: A Layer-2-only access switch (no SVI for VLAN 1 enabled for routing) needs to send management traffic — its own syslog, NTP, and SSH replies — to hosts in different subnets. The switch itself has no routing table; it just needs ONE next-hop for its own management traffic. Which command configures that next hop?
choices: `router ospf 1` + `network` — enables OSPF routing protocol traffic on the switch; it does not configure a management default gateway for the switch CPU's own out-of-band traffic
`ip default-gateway 192.168.1.1` — switch management gateway for the CPU's own traffic
`ip dhcp-server 192.168.1.1` — points at a DHCP server, not a default gateway
`ip routing` + `interface vlan` — turns on L3 forwarding, beyond management need
questions.explanation: 'ip default-gateway' tells the switch where to send its own management traffic (SSH, SNMP) when the destination is off-subnet. It does not enable inter-VLAN routing.

questions.q: An 802.1Q tag carries a 12-bit VID field. Out of the 2^12 = 4096 possible values, VID 0 is reserved (priority-tagged) and VID 4095 is reserved. How many VIDs are usable for normal VLAN assignment in 802.1Q?
choices: 65534 — the ISL legacy trunking range used a different encoding; in 802.1Q the VIDs field is 12-bit, and only VIDs 0 and 4095 are reserved, giving 4094 usable values
4094 — 4096 minus VIDs 0 and 4095 (reserved)
256 — far below 12 bits
questions.explanation: 802.1Q uses a 12-bit VLAN ID field: 2^12 = 4096 values. VLANs 0 and 4095 are reserved, leaving 4094 usable VLANs (1–4094).

questions.q: A single Ethernet link between two switches carries traffic for VLANs 10, 20, and 30. Frames on the link carry a 4-byte tag identifying which VLAN each frame belongs to. The tag format is defined by an IEEE standard. Which standard enables this?
choices: 802.1X — port-based access authentication standard for Ethernet networks; it controls whether a host may use an Ethernet port but is not the VLAN trunk-tagging encapsulation standard
802.3ad — EtherChannel link aggregation, separate concept
802.1Q — VLAN tagging standard for Ethernet trunks
802.11ac — wireless standard, unrelated
questions.explanation: 802.1Q adds a 4-byte tag to Ethernet frames identifying the VLAN. Trunk ports use this tag so a single link can carry frames from multiple VLANs simultaneously.

questions.q: A switch port connecting an unmanaged user PC is configured with `spanning-tree portfast`. Several months later, an end user plugs an unsanctioned switch into that same port to share the desk. Within seconds the access-layer SVI starts flapping and STP topology changes spike. What did PortFast on that port enable to happen?
choices: The port renegotiated to 10 Mbps because PortFast disables auto-negotiation
VLAN tagging was disabled on the port because PortFast strips dot1q headers and the rogue switch cannot signal STP correctly
A Layer-2 loop formed because PortFast skipped STP listening/learning, so the rogue switch's path was forwarded before STP could block it
The port left its EtherChannel bundle because PortFast disables LACP, which prevents a rogue switch from joining the STP topology
questions.explanation: PortFast skips STP Listening and Learning states. If another switch is connected, it bypasses the topology checks that prevent loops. Always pair PortFast with BPDU Guard on edge ports.

questions.q: Two switches bond four 1 G physical links into an 8 Gbps logical interface using a negotiation protocol. The protocol must be vendor-neutral (the switches are from different vendors) and standardised by IEEE. Which protocol fits?
choices: LACP — IEEE 802.3ad / 802.1AX, the open EtherChannel-bundle negotiation protocol
PAgP — Cisco-proprietary EtherChannel negotiation protocol; it is not an IEEE open standard and does not interoperate with non-Cisco equipment
RSTP — spanning-tree, not link aggregation
VTP — VLAN propagation, not link aggregation
questions.explanation: LACP (Link Aggregation Control Protocol, IEEE 802.3ad) is the vendor-neutral standard. PAgP is Cisco-proprietary. Both negotiate EtherChannel formation but LACP works across vendors.

questions.q: A 24-port hub is replaced with a 24-port Layer 2 switch with no VLANs configured (all ports in the default VLAN). How does this change affect collision domains and broadcast domains compared to the hub?
choices: The switch creates 24 separate collision domains (one per port) but all 24 ports remain in a single broadcast domain
The switch creates 24 separate collision domains AND 24 separate broadcast domains — broadcasts are never forwarded between switch ports
The switch eliminates both collision and broadcast domains entirely — each port operates in complete isolation with no shared traffic
Collision domains remain unchanged — both hubs and switches use CSMA/CD, just at different speeds
questions.explanation: A Layer 2 switch creates a separate collision domain per port (full-duplex eliminates collisions entirely on each segment). However, without VLANs, all ports share one broadcast domain — a broadcast frame is still flooded out all ports. To create separate broadcast domains, VLANs or a Layer 3 router are required.

questions.q: Late collisions and CRC errors are climbing on a Gi0/24 access port. A PC plugged into Gi0/24 has its NIC hard-coded to 100/full. The switch port is left at default `speed auto / duplex auto`. Auto-negotiation falls back, and the switch ends up at 100/half while the PC stays at 100/full. Which fix resolves the speed/duplex mismatch correctly?
choices: Hard-code both ends to same speed AND duplex, OR both to auto-negotiate — never mix the two

Swap the PC's NIC — the NIC is unlikely to be at fault; late collisions and CRC errors are the classic symptom of a duplex mismatch caused by hard-coding one of the link ends while leaving the other on auto-negotiate
Enable PortFast on the switch port — PortFast affects STP timing, not the speed / duplex negotiation
Upgrade IOS on the switch — speed / duplex are L1 settings and not influenced by the IOS revision
questions.explanation: Duplex mismatches occur when one side is full-duplex and the other is half-duplex, causing late collisions and errors. The fix is to match settings on both ends — either both auto or both hard-coded identically.

questions.q: An access port receives a tagged frame (802.1Q tag present). What does a Cisco switch do by default?
choices: Forwards the frame normally, ignoring the tag
Sends it to the management VLAN
Strips the tag and assigns the frame to the native VLAN
Drops the frame
questions.explanation: Access ports expect untagged frames. By default, a tagged frame arriving on an access port is dropped. This is a security consideration against VLAN hopping via frame tagging attacks.

nodes.title: Order the DHCP DORA handshake

data.scenario: A new host joins the LAN and needs an IP address. Order the four DHCP messages.

nodes.explanation: A client gets an IP via DORA: Discover (client broadcasts), Offer (server proposes a lease), Request (client asks for it), Acknowledge (server confirms). Release is a separate teardown message, not part of DORA.

nodes.title: Spanning Tree Protocol: Key Ideas
nodes.content: STP prevents loops on Ethernet networks by blocking redundant links. Without it, a single redundant cable between two switches creates a broadcast storm that takes the LAN down. STP automatically picks one root bridge and computes a loop-free tree.

flashcards.front: Why is loop prevention needed on Ethernet?
flashcards.back: Ethernet frames have no TTL — once a broadcast frame enters a loop it circulates forever, doubling on every pass, until the LAN melts. STP detects redundant paths and blocks them, leaving a spanning tree. If the active link fails, STP unblocks an alternate.

flashcards.front: How is the root bridge elected?
flashcards.back: Lowest bridge ID wins. Bridge ID = priority (default 32768, lower is better) followed by MAC address. In practice you set the priority on your core switches so root election is predictable, not whoever happens to have the lowest MAC.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between RSTP and classic STP?
flashcards.back: Classic 802.1D converges in 30-50 seconds (listen → learn → forward). RSTP (802.1w) converges in 1-2 seconds by negotiating port roles between adjacent switches instead of timing them out. Always use RSTP — classic STP is too slow for modern data centers.

flashcards.front: Portfast / Bridge Assurance — when do you enable them?
flashcards.back: PortFast bypasses the listening/learning states on access ports (anywhere an end host plugs in) — link comes up forwarding immediately. NEVER enable PortFast on a switch-to-switch trunk; it lets loops form during reconvergence.

questions.q: STP is enabled on a switch. A port is currently in the Listening state. What does this port do?
choices: Blocks all traffic including BPDUs
Does not forward frames or learn MAC addresses
Forwards frames and learns MAC addresses
Learns MAC addresses but does not forward frames
questions.explanation: In the Listening state, a port processes BPDUs to participate in the STP election, but does NOT forward frames or learn MAC addresses. Learning comes next, then Forwarding.

questions.q: Classic 802.1D STP defined three port roles (Root, Designated, Blocked). RSTP (802.1w) adds two new ROLES so the topology can converge in under a second: one is the next-best path toward the root if the active root port fails; the other is the backup designated port on a shared (e.g. hub) segment. Which two roles are these?
choices: Edge and Non-edge — describe PortFast-related port types in RSTP; they are not the new port-role additions that introduced the backup and alternate forwarding-path concepts
Alternate and Backup
Blocking and Forwarding
Root and Designated
questions.explanation: RSTP introduces the Alternate role (a pre-computed standby for the Root port) and the Backup role (a standby Designated port on a shared segment). Edge/Non-edge are RSTP port types, Blocking/Forwarding are STP states, and Root/Designated are roles that already existed in 802.1D.

questions.q: A spanning-tree topology converges: every non-root switch picks ONE root port toward the same upstream switch and the same set of designated ports. That upstream switch sends the periodic BPDUs that govern the topology. By what mechanism was that upstream switch chosen?
choices: It is the switch with the lowest Bridge ID (priority then MAC) — the STP root
It is the switch with the fastest CPU and forwarding ASIC
It is the L3 router that connects the switched network to the internet
It is whichever switch first sent a topology-change BPDU after boot
questions.explanation: The root bridge is elected based on the lowest Bridge ID (priority + MAC). All other switches calculate their shortest path to the root bridge to determine port roles. all STP paths are calculated relative to it

questions.q: An admin enters `spanning-tree portfast default` in global config so PortFast is applied to every access port at boot. A user plugs a hub into one of those ports and a topology loop forms before STP can react. What did PortFast do that allowed the loop to form?
choices: Forced the port into Blocking state immediately on link-up
Skipped Listening and Learning so the port forwards on link-up
Disabled BPDU transmission across every access port
Set the bridge priority to zero on every access port
questions.explanation: PortFast bypasses STP's Listening and Learning timers so an edge port goes straight to Forwarding the moment a host links up. That's safe for a single endpoint but unsafe if a switch or hub is plugged in — which is why PortFast should be paired with BPDU Guard so any incoming BPDU err-disables the port.

questions.q: Two Catalyst switches form a single logical L2 domain; the one chosen by STP as the reference point — the lowest bridge-ID on the segment — sets all of its ports to the Designated role and other switches calculate their paths toward it. What is this STP role called?
choices: Designated Bridge
Root Bridge
Backup Bridge
Alternate Bridge
questions.explanation: The Root Bridge is the single anchor of an STP topology — every other bridge's Root Port points toward it and Designated Ports flow away from it. 'Designated' applies to ports (and to bridges per segment); 'Backup' and 'Alternate' are RSTP port roles, not bridge titles.

questions.q: Two switches are directly connected. SW1 sends a BPDU with Bridge ID 32769:aabb.cc00.0100. SW2 sends 32769:aabb.cc00.0200. Which becomes the root bridge?
choices: Neither — root election requires a third switch
SW2 — it has a higher MAC
Both are root bridges on different VLANs
SW1 — it wins on lower MAC address
questions.explanation: Bridge ID = priority + MAC address. Both have the same priority (32769), so the lower MAC wins. aabb.cc00.0100 < aabb.cc00.0200, so SW1 becomes the root bridge. giving a lower Bridge ID

questions.q: A network engineer is reviewing the RSTP topology. Switch A has a port that receives the best BPDU from a non-root switch but does not lead toward the root bridge. What port role is assigned to that port?
choices: Alternate port — backup path to root, kept in discarding state
Root port — it provides the best path to the root bridge
Backup port — it is a redundant connection on the same segment
Designated port — it forwards traffic toward the root bridge
questions.explanation: In RSTP, an Alternate port receives a superior BPDU from a neighboring switch (not from the root direction) and is placed in Discarding state as a backup path. If the Root port fails, the Alternate port transitions to Root port quickly without a full topology recalculation.

nodes.title: Cloud fundamentals (CLF-C02 / AZ-900 / CCNA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud fundamentals questions appear on almost every entry-level certification. They test your ability to map a business requirement to the correct service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), understand the provider vs customer responsibility split, and compare on-premises capex to cloud opex — all before any technical deep-dive.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — who manages what in each model?
flashcards.back: IaaS (EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine): provider manages hardware + hypervisor; you manage OS, runtime, app, data. PaaS (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine): provider adds OS + runtime; you manage app + data. SaaS (Office 365, Salesforce): provider manages everything; you manage user config and data. As you move up the stack you trade control for speed.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — where is the exact dividing line?
flashcards.back: The provider is always responsible for security OF the cloud (physical data centers, networking fabric, hypervisor, managed service software). The customer is always responsible for security IN the cloud (data classification, IAM configuration, OS patching on IaaS VMs, application code). The dividing line shifts up the stack for PaaS and SaaS — the more managed the service, the more the provider owns.

flashcards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones — what is each?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic cluster of data centers (e.g., us-east-1, West Europe). An AZ is one or more discrete data centers within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. AZs in a region are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication but far enough apart that a fire/flood in one doesn't hit another. Spread workloads across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud shift the spending model?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): large upfront purchase of hardware that you then depreciate over years; on-premises servers. Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing pay-as-you-go cost; cloud compute bills. Cloud converts infra from capex to opex — no hardware procurement lead times, costs scale with actual usage, easier to budget for a startup or to kill a failed project without a sunk-cost legacy.

questions.q: An IPv4 /26 subnet has 26 bits of network and 6 bits of host. The host range minus the network address minus the broadcast address gives the number of USABLE host addresses on that subnet. How many?
choices: 30 — that's a /27 (5 host bits)
62 — a /26 with 6 host bits: 2^6 − 2 = 64 − 2 = 62 usable hosts
64 — total addresses in a /26 BEFORE subtracting the two non-usable addresses (network and broadcast); usable hosts = 62
questions.explanation: /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 = 64 total addresses. Subtract 1 network + 1 broadcast = 62 usable hosts.

questions.q: An IPv4 subnet uses a /28 prefix. Twenty-eight bits identify the network; four bits remain for hosts. What is the matching subnet mask in dotted-decimal form?
An interface is configured with `ip address 192.168.1.64 255.255.255.192` (i.e. 192.168.1.64/26). What is the directed broadcast address for this subnet?
choices: 192.168.1.255 — the all-hosts broadcast of the /24, not this /26 subnet
192.168.1.95 — would be the broadcast of a /27 starting at .64, not a /26
questions.explanation: /26 = 64 addresses per subnet. Starting at .64, the range ends at .127. The broadcast is 192.168.1.127.

questions.q: Gi0/1 on a switch is connected via a UTP cable to a server's NIC, both sides locked to 1000/full. The link has been up for 24 hours. The interface counters show ZERO collisions, ZERO late collisions, and ZERO CSMA/CD-related events. Why are there no collisions on this link?
choices: Collisions still occur on a full-duplex link but are auto-corrected by the NIC firmware
Full-duplex separates Tx/Rx onto dedicated pairs — no shared medium, no collisions
Collisions are halved (≈50%) at full duplex; the counter rounds them down to zero
CSMA/CD silently manages collisions in the background on full-duplex links
questions.explanation: Full-duplex uses separate TX and RX wires, eliminating collisions entirely. CSMA/CD is disabled in full-duplex mode. Half-duplex shares the medium and uses CSMA/CD.

questions.q: The OSI reference model splits the upper stack into Session (5), Presentation (6), and Application (7) layers. The TCP/IP model collapses all three into a single layer. Which TCP/IP layer corresponds to OSI layers 5, 6, and 7 together?
choices: Internet — the equivalent layer in the TCP/IP model for packet forwarding; it is not one of the OSI model layer names and does not map to the OSI application-specific top layer
Transport
Application
Network Access
questions.explanation: The TCP/IP Application layer absorbs OSI layers 5–7. Protocols that operate there include HTTP, DNS, FTP, and SMTP. Internet aligns with OSI 3, Transport with OSI 4, and Network Access with OSI 1–2.

questions.q: A point-to-point WAN link is allocated a /29 subnet. The /29 has 8 total addresses minus the network (1st) and broadcast (last). How many usable host addresses remain?
choices: 14 — that's /28 (4 host bits), not /29
8 — total addresses in /29 BEFORE subtracting network + broadcast
6 — 8 minus the network and broadcast addresses; correct for /29
4 — that's /30 minus reserved, not /29
questions.explanation: /29 has 3 host bits: 2^3 = 8 total addresses. Subtract network (.0) and broadcast (.7) = 6 usable host addresses.

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.front: What's the standard troubleshooting model?
flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

flashcards.front: Why ask 'what changed recently'?
flashcards.back: Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

flashcards.front: What's the divide-and-conquer technique?
flashcards.back: Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.

questions.q: An engineer runs 'show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0' and sees: 'GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is down'. The cable is verified good and the remote device is powered on. What does this output indicate and what is the MOST likely cause?
choices: Both Layer 1 and Layer 2 have failed — the cable is likely damaged despite visual inspection
The remote device's IP address is unreachable, causing the protocol state to drop
The interface is administratively disabled and needs 'no shutdown' to recover
Layer 1 is functional (signal present) but Layer 2 has failed.
questions.explanation: 'Up/down' means the physical layer is working (carrier detected) but the data link layer cannot establish. Common causes: encapsulation mismatch (e.g., HDLC vs PPP), missing 'clock rate' on a DCE serial interface, or keepalive failures. 'Administratively down/down' would indicate a manual shutdown. likely due to keepalive failure, encapsulation mismatch, or missing clock rate on a serial link

questions.q: A router shows 'GigabitEthernet0/0 up/up' in 'show ip interface brief' and has a valid OSPF route to 10.5.5.0/24 via Gi0/0. Users report they cannot reach the server at 10.5.5.10. Pinging from the router toward 10.5.5.10 returns '!!!!!'. What is the MOST likely cause of the user connectivity problem?
choices: The OSPF route is a summary route and does not cover the specific host 10.5.5.10
An outbound ACL on Gi0/0 blocks user traffic but not the router's own pings, explaining the asymmetry
The router's ARP table has a stale entry for 10.5.5.10 pointing to the wrong MAC address
The spanning tree is blocking the user-facing switch ports, preventing frames from reaching the router
questions.explanation: When the router can ping the destination successfully but users cannot reach it, an outbound ACL on the router's egress interface is a classic culprit. Router-sourced pings use the router's own IP as the source, which may be permitted by the ACL, while user traffic (sourced from user subnet IPs) is blocked. Always check 'show ip access-lists' and 'show ip interface' (which shows applied ACLs) when the router can reach a destination but users cannot.

questions.q: An engineer runs 'show interfaces Gi0/0' and sees 'input errors: 1423, CRC: 1423'. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Duplex mismatch or faulty cable
IP address misconfiguration on the interface
The interface is administratively down
Incorrect VLAN assignment
questions.explanation: CRC errors and input errors are typically caused by a duplex mismatch (one side full, other half-duplex) or a bad/damaged cable. They indicate physical or data link layer problems.

questions.q: An engineer runs `traceroute 8.8.8.8` and sees hops 1-3 reply normally, hops 4-6 show `* * *`, then hop 7 replies with the destination. Two facts are key: (a) the destination replied, so the path is intact; (b) only hops 4-6 don't generate ICMP. What's the most likely explanation?
choices: The path is broken at hop 4
Hops 4-6 silently drop ICMP Time-Exceeded — data path works, only traceroute is suppressed
A routing loop sits between hops 4 and 6; hop 7's reply comes from a different return path
NAT at hop 4 hides hops 5 and 6 and resets the IP TTL counter
questions.explanation: Traceroute works by sending packets with TTL=1, 2, 3... and expecting ICMP Time Exceeded (type 11) messages back from each router. If routers 4-6 have ACLs or firewall rules blocking outbound ICMP Time Exceeded, they will silently discard the TTL-expired packets without responding — causing '* * *'. The packets are still being forwarded, which is why the destination at hop 7 responds. This is extremely common on internet paths where ISP routers filter ICMP.

questions.q: A network engineer pings 192.168.5.1 from a router and receives the output '!!U!U' (where '!' = success and 'U' = destination unreachable). What does the 'U' response specifically indicate?
choices: The ping timed out on those attempts — a timeout means no reply arrived within the window; a timeout is different from a router actively generating an ICMP Destination Unreachable response
The destination host is powered off and an ARP request went unanswered for those packets
A router somewhere along the path actively sent back an ICMP Destination Unreachable message (Type 3).
A firewall along the path is rate-limiting ICMP Echo Replies, causing intermittent success
questions.explanation: In Cisco IOS ping output: '!' = Echo Reply received (success), '.' = timeout (no response), 'U' = ICMP Unreachable received, 'N' = Network Unreachable, 'H' = Host Unreachable, 'Q' = Source Quench. A 'U' means a device along the path actively sent back an ICMP Type 3 (Destination Unreachable), indicating it knows the destination is unreachable (e.g., a deny ACL with 'icmp unreachable' enabled, or no route to host). A '.' (dot/timeout) would indicate no response at all. indicating the destination is known to be unreachable due to no route, an ACL deny, or a wrong subnet

questions.q: `show interfaces Gi0/0` reports the interface as `up / down`. Line protocol DOWN means the L1 link is fine (carrier detected) but L2 keepalives / CDP / handshakes are not arriving. Which root cause class fits an up/down state?
choices: Administratively shutdown — that would show `administratively down / down`, not `up / down`
L2 issue — keepalive failure, encapsulation mismatch, clocking or LMI problem
Missing IP — IP is L3 config and doesn't affect L1/L2 state reporting
Cable unplugged — that would be `down / down`, not `up / down`
questions.explanation: 'Up/down' means Layer 1 is ok (cable, signal) but Layer 2 has failed. Common causes: encapsulation mismatch, keepalive failures, or PPP/HDLC mismatches. 'Admin down/down' means it was manually shut. encapsulation mismatch, or no signal on the line

nodes.title: IPv6 fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IPv6 is the 128-bit successor to IPv4, designed to end address exhaustion while simplifying headers and autoconfiguration. Exams test you on address types, notation, and the concepts that disappeared (NAT, broadcast) or changed (SLAAC, dual-stack).

flashcards.front: How long is an IPv6 address and how is it written?
flashcards.back: 128 bits, written as eight 16-bit groups of hex separated by colons. You may drop leading zeros in a group and replace one run of all-zero groups with :: once per address.

flashcards.front: What are the three main IPv6 address types and what happened to broadcast?
flashcards.back: Unicast (one interface), multicast (one-to-many, prefix ff00::/8), and anycast (delivered to the nearest of a group). IPv6 has no broadcast — its role is handled by multicast.

flashcards.front: What is a link-local address and which range does it use?
flashcards.back: An address valid only on the local link, auto-configured on every IPv6 interface from fe80::/10. It is used for neighbor discovery and next-hop communication and is never routed off-link.

flashcards.front: Compare SLAAC, DHCPv6, and EUI-64.
flashcards.back: SLAAC lets a host build its own address from a router-advertised /64 prefix plus an interface ID; EUI-64 derives that 64-bit interface ID from the MAC (inserting fffe, flipping the U/L bit). DHCPv6 instead assigns addresses/options from a server — stateful or stateless.

questions.q: On a freshly-enabled IPv6 interface — no RA, no DHCPv6 — the host already holds an IPv6 address bearing the FE80::/10 prefix. Packets sourced from that address never leave the segment. Which IPv6 address category is being described?
choices: Unique Local from the FC00::/7 prefix — routable within a site, but requires manual assignment or DHCPv6; it is not automatically generated on every IPv6 interface at startup
Global Unicast from the 2000::/3 prefix
Anycast, drawn from the unicast range
Link-Local, automatic on every IPv6 interface
questions.explanation: Link-local addresses live under FE80::/10 and are auto-configured on every IPv6 interface; their scope is bounded to a single link, which is why packets carrying them are never forwarded. Neighbor discovery and routing-protocol hellos rely on them.

questions.q: On an IPv6 segment, a host needs to resolve a neighbour's link-layer address from its IPv6 address. IPv6 does not run ARP. The host sends a Neighbor Solicitation (ICMPv6 type 135) to the solicited-node multicast and receives a Neighbor Advertisement (ICMPv6 type 136) carrying the link-layer address. Which protocol provides this function?
choices: DHCPv6 — stateful or stateless address configuration
IPv6 ARP
NDP (ICMPv6 discovery) — types 133-137
Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC)
questions.explanation: Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) is the ICMPv6-based replacement for ARP, RA/RS, and parameter discovery. The Neighbor Solicitation / Neighbor Advertisement pair handles link-layer resolution. There is no 'IPv6 ARP'. DHCPv6 assigns addresses, and SLAAC builds an address from an RA prefix — neither performs L2 resolution.

questions.q: A host on a /64 IPv6 LAN comes up. The router on the segment advertises an RA with the A-flag set and no DHCPv6 server is present. The host computes its own 128-bit address: prefix from the RA + an interface identifier derived from its MAC (modified EUI-64) or a random privacy ID. Which IPv6 mechanism is this?
choices: DHCPv6 stateful assignment — server allocates the full address including IID, without random privacy extension; the host uses the server-assigned address, not a self-generated IID combined with the RA prefix
SLAAC — host derives the IID from EUI-64 or random privacy, combines with RA prefix
IPv4-mapped IPv6 address — uses the IPv4 address as the IID; not what SLAAC does
Manual interface-ID assignment — admin-set; SLAAC is automatic
questions.explanation: SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) uses the prefix from Router Advertisements plus an EUI-64 interface identifier (or RFC 7217 random value) to self-configure a global IPv6 address.

questions.q: An IPv6 service is anchored at IP 2001:db8::1, configured on routers in five POPs around the world. Clients send packets to 2001:db8::1 and the network delivers each packet to the GEOGRAPHICALLY NEAREST instance. Which IPv6 address category enables one address shared by many interfaces?
choices: Anycast — one address on multiple interfaces, routes to the topologically nearest
Link-local — FE80::/10, automatically configured on every IPv6 interfaces; it is a per-link address, not a shared anycast address reachable from multiple geographically distributed interfaces
Multicast — FF::/8, delivered to ALL members, not the nearest one
Global unicast — assigned to exactly ONE interface globally, opposite of anycast
questions.explanation: An anycast address is assigned to multiple interfaces. Packets sent to an anycast address are delivered to the topologically nearest interface with that address. Used for DNS and CDN redundancy.

questions.q: A network engineer assigns the IPv6 address 2001:0db8:abcd::1/64 to a router interface. Which address type does this represent?
choices: Link-local address — automatically generated and valid only on the local segment
Unique Local Address — used for private internal routing, not routable on the internet
Global Unicast Address — routable on the public IPv6 internet
Anycast address — assigned to multiple interfaces for load sharing
questions.explanation: 2001:db8::/32 is within the Global Unicast Address range (2000::/3). Global Unicast Addresses are publicly routable. Note: 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation; real GUAs are assigned by IANA/RIRs. Link-local begins with FE80::/10 and Unique Local with FC00::/7.

nodes.title: Wireless networking: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Wi-Fi exam questions cluster around standards (which band, which speed), authentication modes (Open / WPA2-PSK / WPA3-Enterprise), and troubleshooting (interference, channel overlap, weak signal vs slow client). Knowing the practical defaults beats memorizing every spec.

flashcards.front: 2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz vs 6 GHz — pick the right band.
flashcards.back: 2.4 GHz: longer range, slower, more congestion (every microwave, baby monitor, BT device). 5 GHz: faster, shorter range, more channels (less crowded). 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E): newest, very fast, very clean, but client support is recent. Modern APs broadcast all three; clients auto-pick. For dense environments, prefer 5 GHz with 20 MHz channels.

flashcards.front: WPA2-PSK vs WPA2-Enterprise — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: PSK: one shared password for the whole SSID — easy, fine for home/small office. Cannot revoke a single user without rotating the PSK for everyone. Enterprise (802.1X/EAP): each user authenticates with their own credentials against a RADIUS server backed by AD/LDAP — required for compliance, audit, individual revocation. Always Enterprise at work.

flashcards.front: What is channel overlap and how do you avoid it?
flashcards.back: Adjacent 2.4 GHz channels overlap; only 1, 6, 11 are non-overlapping in North America. If three APs use 1, 6, 7 instead of 1, 6, 11, channel 7 collides with both 6 and 11 — throughput drops everywhere. Site-survey, pick non-overlapping channels, enable Auto-RF features (DCA, TPC) on modern controllers.

flashcards.front: Slow Wi-Fi — what's the troubleshooting order?
flashcards.back: (1) Confirm it's wireless: try wired. (2) Check signal strength (RSSI > -67 dBm is fine, < -75 is bad). (3) Check channel utilization (a busy channel = airtime starvation). (4) Check client capability (an old 2.4-GHz-only laptop won't reach Wi-Fi 6 speeds). (5) Check the AP-uplink (gigabit AP connected to a 100 Mbps switch port is a classic bottleneck).

questions.q: A wireless engineer is choosing equipment for a high-density office. The vendor data sheet for 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) shows OFDM modulation, 80 / 160 MHz channels, and only one supported frequency band — not the same band as legacy 802.11b/g/n. On which band does 802.11ac operate?
choices: 5 GHz only — 802.11ac is a 5-GHz standard (legacy 2.4 was 802.11b/g/n)
Both 2.4 and 5 GHz
2.4 GHz only
6 GHz only
questions.explanation: 802.11ac operates exclusively on 5 GHz. 802.11n operates on both bands. Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) adds 6 GHz support.

questions.q: During a wireless security assessment, an engineer captures a WPA2-Personal 4-way handshake from a corporate SSID using a passive Wi-Fi adapter without ever associating with the network. What attack can now be performed completely offline?
choices: Offline dictionary or brute-force attack against the captured handshake to recover the Pre-Shared Key.
Replay attack — injecting the captured handshake back onto the network; this does not perform any offline cryptanalysis and cannot recover the Pre-Shared Key
KRACK (Key Reinstallation Attack) — the captured handshake provides the key material needed to decrypt existing sessions
Deauthentication attack — sending the captured handshake back forces all clients to disconnect from the AP
questions.explanation: WPA2-Personal's 4-way handshake contains enough information to attempt offline password cracking. Tools like hashcat or aircrack-ng can test millions of passwords per second against the captured handshake without any further network access. This is why WPA2-Personal with short or dictionary-based PSKs is weak. WPA3 with SAE (Dragonfly) prevents this by providing forward secrecy and resistance to offline attacks. success depends entirely on password complexity

questions.q: A campus is moving away from each access point having its own SSID/policy config. The new model places one or more controllers in the data centre; APs build a CAPWAP tunnel to a controller, controllers push the SSID, RF, and security policy, and APs become 'lightweight' devices that only handle radio and bridging. Which WLAN architecture is this?
choices: Mesh deployment with a root AP and wireless backhaul between sibling APs — APs in a mesh do not run as lightweight CAPWAP clients tunnelling to a central WLC controller; they forward traffic autonomously across the backhaul
Cloud-managed AP architecture where each AP individually talks to a SaaS dashboard, no on-prem WLC
Autonomous (standalone) AP mode where each AP holds its own full configuration
Centralised controller-based architecture (WLC + lightweight APs over CAPWAP)
questions.explanation: In controller-based architectures, lightweight APs (LWAP) tunnel all traffic to a Wireless LAN Controller (WLC) via CAPWAP. The WLC handles authentication, roaming, RF management, and policy centrally.

questions.q: A company is deploying a wireless network and wants to use the strongest commercially available encryption with support for Protected Management Frames. Which wireless security standard should they choose?
choices: WEP with 128-bit key — the extended key length provides adequate security for enterprise use
WPA2-Enterprise with CCMP — it provides stronger encryption but does not support management frame protection
WPA3 with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) and mandatory PMF.
WPA2-Personal with TKIP — it is backward-compatible and supports all legacy clients
questions.explanation: WPA3 replaces the PSK four-way handshake with SAE (Dragonfly handshake), which provides forward secrecy and resistance to offline dictionary attacks. WPA3 also mandates Protected Management Frames (PMF/802.11w), protecting against deauthentication attacks. WPA2 with CCMP/AES is still strong but does not mandate PMF or offer forward secrecy. providing forward secrecy and stronger handshake protection

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: VTP mode 'transparent' is configured on a switch. How does it handle VTP advertisements received on a trunk?
choices: It becomes the VTP server for the domain
Forwards VTP ads without applying them locally
It drops all VTP advertisements
It processes and applies the VLAN changes locally
questions.explanation: VTP transparent mode forwards VTP advertisements to maintain backward compatibility, but does not synchronize its own VLAN database. It manages its VLANs independently.

questions.q: A switch port is configured as an access port in VLAN 30. It receives a frame without an 802.1Q tag. What happens?
choices: The frame is dropped
The frame is assigned to VLAN 30
The port shuts down
The frame is treated as VLAN 1 traffic
questions.explanation: Access ports don't expect 802.1Q tags. Any untagged frame arriving on an access port is automatically associated with the configured access VLAN (VLAN 30 in this case).

questions.q: A trunk between SW1 and SW2 carries VLAN 10, 20, 30 and is configured with `switchport trunk native vlan 99`. A PC sends an untagged Ethernet frame onto the trunk. SW2 receives that untagged frame on the trunk interface. To which VLAN does SW2 assign the frame?
choices: VLAN 1, because untagged frames always use the trunk's native VLAN
Nowhere — the frame is dropped because trunks discard untagged traffic
VLAN 99, the native VLAN of the trunk
VLAN 10, 20, and 30 simultaneously across the allowed list
questions.explanation: By definition, the native VLAN is the one to which untagged traffic on a trunk is assigned. Both ends must agree on the native VLAN or frames will be misclassified. Best practice: set the native VLAN to an unused value so a misconfigured access port can't leak into VLAN 1.

questions.q: You must connect a switch port to a printer that does NOT support DTP. Which TWO commands belong on the switch interface to lock it as an access port and stop trunk negotiation?
choices: switchport mode trunk — sets the port as a tagged VLAN trunk rather than an access port; a printer port must be in access mode, not trunk mode
switchport mode access
switchport nonegotiate
no switchport
questions.explanation: `switchport mode access` forces the port into access mode (no trunk). `switchport nonegotiate` disables DTP frames so the port never tries to negotiate trunking with the connected device. `switchport mode trunk` would do the opposite, and `no switchport` makes the port a routed L3 interface.

questions.q: An admin needs Layer-2 neighbour discovery in a multi-vendor environment where Cisco's proprietary CDP isn't available on every device. The replacement must run over Ethernet, publish device identity and capability TLVs, and be supported across Cisco / HP / Juniper / Arista. Which protocol fits?
choices: SNMP — the vendor-neutral standard for MIB-based device management over UDP; it is not a Layer-2 link-layer neighbour-discovery protocol
NetFlow — flow-level telemetry, not L2 discovery
LLDP (IEEE 802.1AB) — vendor-neutral L2 discovery protocol
RSPAN — remote port mirroring, not discovery
questions.explanation: LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol, IEEE 802.1AB) is the open standard equivalent of Cisco's CDP. Both advertise device identity, capabilities, and neighbor information at Layer 2.

questions.q: A NOC is replacing legacy SNMPv1/v2c with SNMPv3 across thousands of devices. The CISO wants two things v3 provides that v1/v2c do not: cryptographic authentication of every message and optional encryption of the payload. Which SNMPv3 security mode covers both?
choices: authPriv — authentication (HMAC) + privacy (AES/DES) for SNMP
Increased polling frequency — sends more SNMP queries per second; it has no effect on message authentication, integrity, or privacy
Native IPv6 OID support — irrelevant to message security
Larger MIB schema — irrelevant to message security
questions.explanation: SNMPv3 adds user-based security: authentication (MD5/SHA) prevents tampering, and privacy (DES/AES) encrypts the payload. SNMPv1 and v2c use community strings in cleartext.

questions.q: An engineer enables a neighbour-discovery protocol on a campus that mixes Cisco, HP, and Juniper switches. The protocol must be the open, IEEE-defined alternative to Cisco's CDP — not proprietary, runs at Layer 2, advertises identity / capability / system-description TLVs. Which statement correctly compares LLDP to CDP?
choices: CDP discovers non-Cisco devices natively
LLDP (IEEE 802.1AB) is vendor-neutral — works across Cisco, HP, Juniper, Arista, etc.
Both LLDP and CDP are Layer-3 IP-multicast protocols
LLDP is Cisco-proprietary and CDP is the IEEE open standard
questions.explanation: LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol, IEEE 802.1AB) is the open standard equivalent of CDP. Both operate at Layer 2 using multicast frames to advertise device identity, capabilities, and port information. CDP only works between Cisco devices; LLDP works across all vendors, making it the preferred choice in mixed-vendor environments. while CDP is Cisco-proprietary and works only between Cisco devices

questions.q: An extended ACL must filter traffic from host 10.1.1.1 to web server 10.2.2.2 on port 80. Where should it be applied?
choices: On the core switch uplink
Outbound on the destination interface
Inbound, as close to the destination as possible
Inbound, as close to the source as possible
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs can match source, destination, and port. Place them near the source so unwanted traffic is dropped early and bandwidth is not wasted traversing the network.
